method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar sits near its highest since April 2025 because markets expect a Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9, though bets on a larger half-point rise faded after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned on Sunday, November 22 against raising rates too far. October PCE inflation on Wednesday, November 25 is the week's test.

EUR.text: The euro slipped below $1.10 on Thursday, November 19, its lowest since April 2025, because the Federal Reserve looks set to keep raising rates faster than the European Central Bank. Firm words on Friday, November 20 from Bundesbank head Joachim Nagel back a December ECB rise but do little against worry about France's April presidential election and the wider rate gap with the US.

GBP.text: UK shop sales rose a strong 0.7% in October, reported on Friday, November 20, which helps the pound and supports another Bank of England rate rise in December. That partly undoes the softer core inflation reading of Wednesday, November 18, though the pound still trades near its lowest against the dollar in about a month.

JPY.text: The yen firmed on Friday, November 20 as US stocks fell hard and US 10-year yields dropped below 5%, and most economists expect a Bank of Japan rate rise to 1.50% on December 18. The wide gap between US and Japanese rates still keeps the dollar near 159 yen, and Tokyo prices on Thursday, November 26 are the next clue.

CHF.text: The Swiss franc sits near a one-month low against a dollar lifted by bets on more Federal Reserve rate rises. A deep fall in US stocks on Friday, November 20, Iran's claim on Sunday, November 22 that two tankers hit sea mines, and President Trump's threat the same day to restart strikes on Iran after the New Year add some demand for the franc as a safe place.

CAD.text: The Canadian dollar sits near 69.8 US cents, close to its weakest since April 2025, because markets expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates faster than the Bank of Canada. Canada's retail sales report on Friday, November 20 pointed to a drop in October, and oil sliding toward $90 the same day cuts Canada's export income too.

AUD.text: The Australian dollar sits near 66 US cents, close to its lowest since January, after Australia lost jobs for a second month and an early business survey on Monday, November 23 showed activity shrinking at its fastest pace in more than five years. Both make another Reserve Bank of Australia rate rise on December 8 less likely, and October inflation on Wednesday, November 25 is the last big test.

NZD.text: The New Zealand dollar sits near 55 US cents, close to its lowest since the pandemic, held down by a US dollar lifted by expected Federal Reserve rate rises. A strong jump in shop sales for July to September, reported on Monday, November 23, makes more Reserve Bank of New Zealand rate cuts less likely and gives the currency some support.

XAU.text: Gold ended Friday, November 20 near $3,538 an ounce after briefly touching $3,503, its lowest since September 2025, closing its worst week since March. Expected Federal Reserve rate rises and a strong dollar outweigh the Iran war, and gold was sold alongside shares in the US stock slide rather than bought as a safe place.

OIL.text: Brent crude slipped to about $92 a barrel as trading reopened on Sunday, November 22, after three weekly falls, because Gulf exports remain strong and a supply surplus is forecast. Attacks on tankers near Hormuz at the war's fastest pace, Iran's claim of two supertankers hitting sea mines and President Trump's threat to strike Iran again after the New Year keep the risk of lost supply in the price.

items.headline: Australian business activity shrinks at its fastest pace in more than five years
items.story_title: Will the RBA raise rates again in December?
items.summary: S&P Global's early survey of Australian purchasing managers for November, out on Monday, November 23 (local time), fell to 46.1 from 48.2, with services at 46.2 and factories at 48.7. Any reading under 50 means activity is shrinking.

beats.was: Australia had already lost jobs for two months in a row, and the Reserve Bank of Australia was split at its November meeting on whether to keep raising rates.
beats.happened: Firms reported falling output, the first drop in new orders in five months, more job cuts and their weakest outlook in three years, while their costs and selling prices rose more slowly.
beats.means: A shrinking economy with cooling price pressure gives the Reserve Bank of Australia more reason to stop raising rates at its December 8 meeting.
beats.fx: Fewer expected rate rises in Australia, while the Federal Reserve keeps signalling more, weigh on the Australian dollar.

impact.why: A deeper slump in business activity lowers the odds of another Australian rate rise.

items.watch: Australia's October inflation figure on Wednesday, November 25, the last big reading before the Reserve Bank of Australia meets on December 8.

items.headline: The dollar eases slightly from its highest in 19 months as Asian trading starts
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The dollar slipped a touch from its highest since April 2025 as trading began in Asia on Monday, November 23. Futures still put about an 89% chance on a quarter-point Federal Reserve rate rise on December 9, but bets on a larger half-point rise have gone.

beats.was: The dollar climbed to its highest in about a year and a half last week as markets came to expect another Federal Reserve rate rise in December and US stocks fell sharply.
beats.happened: The euro edged up to about $1.097, the Australian dollar to about 66.3 US cents, and the dollar rose slightly to about 158.6 yen, with Japan's markets shut for a holiday.
beats.means: Markets still expect one more Fed rise in December, but no longer a bigger one, after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned against raising rates too far.
beats.fx: Smaller rate-rise bets take a little steam out of the dollar, though it stays near its highs.

impact.why: Bets on a larger Fed rate rise in December have faded, a small loss of support for the dollar.
The euro edges up as the dollar eases slightly.

items.watch: US October PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred price gauge, on Wednesday, November 25, ahead of the Fed meeting of December 8 to 9.

items.headline: New Zealand shop sales jump 2.2% in the third quarter
items.story_title: New Zealand's economy and the RBNZ
items.summary: Statistics New Zealand said on Monday, November 23 (local time) that the volume of retail sales rose 2.2% in July to September, more than four times the 0.5% economists expected, after a fall in April to June.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has held its rate at 2.75% while the New Zealand dollar sits near its lowest since the pandemic, and spending had shrunk in the second quarter.
beats.happened: Shoppers bought clearly more in the third quarter, and the value of sales rose in every region of the country.
beats.means: New Zealand households are spending more than expected, which makes further rate cuts from the Reserve Bank less likely.
beats.fx: A firmer economy gives the New Zealand dollar some support against a strong US dollar.

impact.why: A large beat on spending lowers the odds of more rate cuts in New Zealand.

items.watch: Whether the New Zealand dollar holds its gain as Asian markets open, with Japan closed for a holiday on Monday, November 23.

items.headline: China, South Korea and Taiwan move to calm stock markets after the US slide
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: Ahead of Monday, November 23, China eased margin rules for stock buyers, South Korea readied its market stabilisation fund for the first time since 2008, and Taiwan widened limits on short selling after its worst week in 35 years.

beats.was: The S&P 500 fell into a correction last week and the Nasdaq 100 had its worst week since March 2020, as worries about artificial-intelligence spending spread to Asian chip stocks.
beats.happened: Asian governments stepped in with measures to support their stock markets, while Asian shares stood about 18% below their June peak, near a bear market. Japan's markets are closed on Monday, November 23 for a holiday.
beats.means: Officials are worried enough to act, but the fear in markets has not yet eased, and Asian trading may stay rough.
beats.fx: Continued stock market fear tends to help the yen and Swiss franc and hurt currencies tied to global growth, such as the Australian dollar.

impact.why: Weak Asian stock markets weigh on a currency tied to regional growth.
Stock market fear adds some demand for the yen as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether the support steps steady Asian shares through Monday, November 23, and how US stocks open after last week's slide.

items.headline: Bessent warns the Fed against raising rates too far
items.story_title: The Federal Reserve's rate rises
items.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CBS's Face the Nation on Sunday, November 22 that the Federal Reserve could make a policy mistake if it raises rates too much, after US stocks fell into a correction.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve raised its rate to 3.75%-4.00% in September, and markets now almost fully expect another quarter-point rise on December 9.
beats.happened: Bessent pointed to tough talk from Fed governors and a sharp tightening in borrowing conditions as stocks slid. He has made similar points in TV interviews on November 13 and 20.
beats.means: The government is pushing back against more Fed rate rises, but the Fed sets rates on its own and this does not change its plan by itself.
beats.fx: Adds a little doubt to the case for bigger Fed rises, which takes some shine off the dollar.

impact.why: Treasury pressure against more rate rises slightly lowers the odds of a bigger Fed move, though a December rise is still expected.

items.watch: Whether Fed officials answer Bessent before Thanksgiving on Thursday, November 26, and October's PCE inflation on Wednesday, November 25.

items.headline: Trump says he leans toward new strikes on Iran after New Year if talks fail
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Sunday, November 22 that he is inclined to restart strikes on Iran after the New Year if indirect talks bring no deal, and that Iranian ships trying to break the US naval blockade would be sunk.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in February, a framework deal was signed in June, and fighting has flared on and off since July while the US Navy blocks Iran's ports.
beats.happened: Trump dismissed Iran's negotiators as stalling and said US forces would fire on any vessel that tries to cross the blockade. Qatar is passing messages between the two sides.
beats.means: Talks look shakier, and the risk of a bigger war in early 2027 has gone up, though nothing has changed on the water yet.
beats.fx: Keeps a risk premium in oil and some demand for safe currencies as markets reopen.

impact.why: A threat of renewed US strikes raises the chance of more lost Gulf supply, but it is a warning, not an action.
More war risk adds some demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether an Iranian tanker tries to cross the blockade, and any sign of progress or collapse in the Qatar-relayed talks.

items.headline: Iran says two supertankers hit sea mines near Hormuz
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's navy said on Sunday, November 22 that two supertankers struck sea mines and stopped after sailing into a zone it bars near the Strait of Hormuz. The UK's maritime security agency separately reported a tanker in an incident with military forces in the Gulf of Oman, off Chabahar in Iran.

beats.was: The US-Iran war began in late February, and the US Navy has blocked Iran's oil exports for months while Iran has stepped up attacks on other countries' tankers.
beats.happened: Iranian media quoting the Revolutionary Guards navy said two very large tankers caught fire after hitting mines north of Ghanam Island and east of the strait. The ships were not named and the claim has not been confirmed. The UK agency's report came the same day as word that an Iranian tanker may have left Kharg Island to try to slip past the US blockade.
beats.means: If mines are now in the sea lanes, crossing Hormuz gets much riskier for every tanker, not just those Iran picks out.
beats.fx: Adds to the risk of lost Gulf oil just before markets reopen, which supports oil and safe currencies.

impact.why: Mines near the strait would threaten a route that carries a large share of the world's oil, though Iran's claim is not yet confirmed.
A new kind of threat to shipping adds some demand for the franc as a safe place.
Higher oil prices lift Canada's export income.

items.watch: Whether shipping firms or the US Navy confirm the mine strikes and name the ships, and how oil trades once markets reopen on the evening of Sunday, November 22.

items.headline: Attacks on ships around Hormuz are running at the war's highest pace
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: A CNN count of UK maritime reports, published on Sunday, November 22, finds at least 22 attacks on ships near Hormuz so far in November, after more than 30 in October, against about 10 a month earlier in the war. Ship-tracker Kpler says Iranian oil afloat outside the US blockade has fallen to zero.

beats.was: The US-Iran war began in late February, and the US Navy has blocked Iran's oil exports for months while Gulf exports from other countries recovered and oil prices fell.
beats.happened: Reported attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf and the Gulf of Oman jumped in October and stayed high in November. Three tankers leaving the strait were hit on Friday, November 20 and Saturday, November 21, which a risk firm called likely Iranian work.
beats.means: Iran is losing its oil income to the blockade and is pushing back by making the sea route riskier for everyone else.
beats.fx: Keeps a war-risk floor under oil even as Gulf exports recover, and adds some steady demand for safe currencies.

impact.why: More attacks on tankers raise the risk of lost Gulf barrels, though exports have kept flowing so far.
A rising pace of attacks keeps some safe-haven demand for the franc.

items.watch: Whether November's attack count passes October's, and whether insurers or shippers start avoiding the strait again.

items.headline: Iran's Guards say they hit US air-defence radars in Bahrain
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Sunday, November 22 that missiles and drones destroyed two US Patriot air-defence radars at bases in Bahrain, home of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet. The claim has not been confirmed.

beats.was: Bahrain said an Iranian strike on Saturday, November 21 set fire to a civilian industrial site, one of several Iranian attacks around the Gulf in the past week.
beats.happened: The Guards called the radar strikes payback for a US strike on an Iranian radar on Hengam Island. UK maritime data showed ship crossings of Hormuz fell 15% in the week to November 18, with oil tankers down to 37 from 52.
beats.means: Iran is now aiming directly at US forces in a Gulf state, which widens the war beyond attacks on ships.
beats.fx: Raises the chance of a larger US-Iran clash, a mild push for oil and safe currencies.

impact.why: Strikes on US bases in the Gulf raise the risk of a wider war near oil routes, though the damage is unconfirmed.
Direct attacks on US forces add some safe-haven demand.

items.watch: Whether the US confirms damage in Bahrain or answers with new strikes on Iran.

items.headline: Oil slips at the start of the week as strong Gulf exports and a supply surplus outweigh Iran's attacks
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Brent crude fell 0.8% to about $91.85 a barrel as trading reopened late on Sunday, November 22, even after a weekend of Iranian and Houthi attacks around the Gulf, including a Houthi claim of a strike on Saudi Arabia's Rabigh refinery.

beats.was: Brent is down about 20% in November after President Trump held off new strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections, and Gulf exports have stayed close to pre-war levels.
beats.happened: Oil fell despite Trump saying he leans toward new strikes on Iran after the New Year if talks fail, fresh Iranian attacks on Bahrain, and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
beats.means: Traders are giving more weight to a coming supply surplus, about 2 million barrels a day in the last quarter according to the International Energy Agency, than to the war's threats so far.
beats.fx: Softer oil trims export income for Canada and Norway and eases fuel costs for importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Strong Gulf exports and a forecast surplus outweigh the weekend's attacks.
Lower oil prices cut Canada's export income.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29 on output, and whether ship crossings through Hormuz keep falling.

items.headline: Fewer ships cross Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: About 25 tankers have been hit near Hormuz in the week to Sunday, November 22, Al Jazeera reports, and ships crossing the strait fell 15% in the week of November 12-18, with oil tankers down from 52 to 37. Iran also said it shot down another US drone that same day.

beats.was: Since the war began in late February, the US Navy has blocked Iran's oil exports, and traffic through the strait had been recovering toward pre-war levels.
beats.happened: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they hit US radar sites in Bahrain on Saturday, November 21 and downed a fourth US drone in 24 hours on Sunday, November 22. UK maritime data show 263 ships crossed the strait in the week of November 12-18, well below the roughly 135 a day before the war.
beats.means: The rise in attacks is starting to show up in traffic, the first sign in weeks that Gulf oil flows could shrink again.
beats.fx: Backs oil and the currencies that gain from it, like the Canadian dollar, and hurts big oil buyers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Tanker crossings fell by about a quarter in one week, a real hit to the supply that had been coming back.
Japan imports almost all its oil, so a pricier, scarcer supply weighs on the yen.
Canada exports oil, so tighter Gulf supply helps its income.

items.watch: Next week's UK maritime count of crossings, to see whether traffic falls further.

items.headline: Saudi air defences destroy a Houthi drone flying toward Riyadh on Sunday, November 22
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Saudi air defences shot down a Houthi drone headed for Riyadh on Sunday, November 22, hours after stopping a missile aimed at the kingdom's Red Sea coast. No damage or injuries were reported.

beats.was: Yemen's Houthi group, which is backed by Iran, has been firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia during the Iran war, and one hit the Saudi wealth fund's tower in Riyadh on Thursday, November 19.
beats.happened: Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said air defences destroyed a Houthi drone flying toward Riyadh. Earlier the same day the coalition stopped a ballistic missile aimed at the west coast, home to the Yanbu oil export terminal and the Jazan refinery.
beats.means: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia now come almost daily, so the threat to Saudi oil sites stays real even though these strikes caused no harm.
beats.fx: Adds a little to the war risk in oil before markets reopen, with no supply lost.

impact.why: Houthi fire near Saudi oil sites keeps supply risk alive, though nothing was hit.
More Gulf attacks add a little demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether a Houthi strike damages a Saudi oil terminal or refinery, which would hit supply rather than just raise the risk.

items.headline: An Iranian tanker said to be running the US blockade turns out to be a fake signal
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Ship-tracking data seemed to show an Iranian tanker sailing through the Strait of Hormuz past the US blockade, but the monitoring group TankerTrackers said on Sunday, November 22 that the ship does not exist. More than 14 tankers still wait at Iran's Kharg Island oil terminal.

beats.was: The US Navy has blocked Iran's oil exports for 130 days in a row, and Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday, November 20 that the blockade must be broken.
beats.happened: Public ship-tracking signals showed a tanker named Khat-Shekan moving through the strait. TankerTrackers called it a spoof, saying satellite pictures showed no such ship.
beats.means: Iran has not yet broken the blockade, so its oil stays bottled up at Kharg Island and the tanker convoy there is still only a threat.
beats.fx: Takes a little heat out of fears of a sea clash before markets reopen, but leaves Iran's oil off the market.

impact.why: No blockade run means no clash yet, but Iranian barrels stay off the market.

items.watch: Whether the tankers gathered at Kharg Island actually sail, which would test the US Navy directly.

items.headline: Iran says it alone controls Hormuz as a Houthi missile is shot down over western Saudi Arabia
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: On Sunday, November 22 Iran's army said Tehran, not foreign navies, controls the Strait of Hormuz and called that a block to peace talks. Saudi-led forces said they shot down a Houthi missile fired at western Saudi Arabia.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. The US now blockades Iranian ports and escorts ships through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, while Iran says ships must ask its permission to pass.
beats.happened: A day after Iran's attack on Bahrain, Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Iran controls the strait and that this stands in the way of talks to end the war. Separately, the Saudi-led coalition said it stopped a ballistic missile from Yemen's Houthi group aimed at the kingdom's west, and a brief danger alert for Mecca province was lifted. Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said no change has been made to Iran's ban on nuclear weapons, though he admitted some at home argue for one.
beats.means: Neither side is offering a path to a ceasefire, so the risk to Gulf shipping stays in place going into the new week. The words add little new on their own, since nothing was hit and no oil route was closed.
beats.fx: Keeps a small war premium in oil and a little support for safe currencies when markets reopen.

impact.why: Iran's claim over Hormuz and more Houthi fire keep the risk to Gulf supply alive, though no supply was lost.
No sign of peace talks keeps some demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether Iran tries to stop escorted ships in the strait, and how oil trades when markets reopen on the evening of Sunday, November 22.

items.headline: Oil heads into a quiet holiday week with an OPEC+ output meeting set for Sunday, November 29
items.story_title: Oil supply: Gulf flows vs war risk
items.summary: Brent ended Friday, November 20 at $92.57 a barrel after a third weekly fall. The next big date for oil is the OPEC+ ministers' meeting on Sunday, November 29, which sets output plans for 2027.

beats.was: Oil prices jumped when the war with Iran began in late February, but they have fallen for three weeks in a row because tankers are again moving close to pre-war amounts out of the Gulf.
beats.happened: Brent rose 0.6% on Friday, November 20 but still lost about 3.4% on the week. OPEC+, the group of big oil producers led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, meets on Sunday, November 29 to set 2027 output using a fresh review of how much each member can pump. The January Brent contract also expires on Monday, November 30, and the next one trades about $2.60 lower.
beats.means: With US markets closed on Thursday, November 26 for Thanksgiving, trading may be thin, so attacks on ships can move prices more than usual. Until the OPEC+ meeting, supply news from the Gulf is the main driver.
beats.fx: Mixed for oil. The oil price feeds straight into the Canadian dollar, and cheaper oil eases inflation worries in Japan and Europe.

impact.why: A preview: OPEC+ could add or hold supply, while Gulf attacks keep some risk in the price.
Canada's export income follows the oil price, which has no clear push until the OPEC+ meeting.

items.watch: What OPEC+ decides on Sunday, November 29, and whether the attacks on tankers near Hormuz slow Gulf exports again.

items.headline: Iranian attack sets an industrial site in Bahrain on fire as Iran says it aimed at US bases
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Bahrain said an Iranian attack late on Saturday, November 21 hit a civilian industrial site and started a fire, with damage but no injuries. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they fired missiles and drones at US military bases in Bahrain.

beats.was: Bahrain, a small Gulf island state, hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet and has been a target since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. After weeks of calm, it faced three drone attacks in the days before Saturday, November 21.
beats.happened: Bahrain's military said its air defences stopped several Iranian attacks late on Saturday, November 21, but one hit a civilian industrial site, which caught fire. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they targeted US positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases and destroyed two Patriot air-defence radars, a claim not confirmed by the US. Iran called it a reply to US drone flights over its land.
beats.means: Iran is widening its attacks from ships near Hormuz to a Gulf state that hosts US forces, which raises the chance of a US strike back. Markets were shut for the weekend, so the first reaction comes when trading reopens on the evening of Sunday, November 22.
beats.fx: Adds war risk to oil and a little demand for safe currencies such as the yen and Swiss franc.

impact.why: An attack on Gulf soil, not just ships, raises the risk that the war hits oil supply again.
Worries about a wider war add demand for the franc as a safe place.
Some investors buy the yen when war risk rises.

items.watch: Whether the US answers the attack on its bases in Bahrain, and how oil opens on the evening of Sunday, November 22.

items.headline: Two more tankers are hit in the Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens its hold on shipping
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Two tankers were struck by unknown projectiles off Oman's Khasab coast on Saturday, November 21, with no one hurt. Iran said a separate tanker hit a sea mine east of the strait after ignoring its warnings.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane between Iran and Oman that carried about a fifth of the world's oil before the war, has seen ships hit almost daily in November. Iran wants ships to follow lanes it sets, and the US has answered by blockading Iran's ports and escorting tankers.
beats.happened: The UK Maritime Trade Operations, a British navy office that tracks shipping risks, reported one tanker hit at the rear about 20 km north of Khasab and another hit in the engine room about 31 km east, within an hour. Iran's navy said a tanker that had switched off its tracking gear hit a mine and caught fire, which could not be checked independently.
beats.means: Iran's own military counts about 25 tanker incidents in the week to Saturday, November 21. So far oil keeps flowing near pre-war levels, which is why prices fell for three weeks, but each hit raises shipping and insurance costs.
beats.fx: A small lift for oil against its recent slide, and a little support for safe currencies.

impact.why: More ships hit near Hormuz, though exports have kept flowing so far.
Ongoing attacks keep some demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether any ship owners stop sending tankers through Hormuz, and whether the US changes how it escorts them.

items.headline: A short US week puts the Fed's preferred inflation gauge up on Wednesday, November 25
items.story_title: Fed rate rises
items.summary: The Thanksgiving week packs most US data into Wednesday, November 25, led by October's PCE inflation, the measure the Federal Reserve targets. Futures show a near-certain quarter-point Fed rate rise on Wednesday, December 9.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising rates to fight inflation pushed up by the oil shock from the Iran war, and its October meeting minutes showed nearly all officials expect more rises. That has lifted the dollar to its highest since April 2025.
beats.happened: Monday, November 23 brings early business surveys (PMIs) for Germany, the euro area, the UK and the US. Wednesday, November 25 brings October PCE inflation, expected to show prices excluding food and energy up 0.3% on the month with the yearly rate rising to about 3.2%, plus revised third-quarter growth, durable goods orders, the Fed's Beige Book and Australia's October inflation. US markets close on Thursday, November 26 and shut early on Friday, November 27.
beats.means: A PCE reading at or above forecast would back the December rate rise markets already expect. A softer one could trim talk of a bigger move or of further rises in 2027.
beats.fx: A firm PCE reading would support the dollar, while a soft one would ease some of its lift.

impact.why: A preview: the PCE reading could confirm or soften the expected December Fed rise.
Australia's October inflation on Wednesday, November 25 shapes the Reserve Bank of Australia's next move.

items.watch: October core PCE on Wednesday, November 25: above 0.3% on the month would firm bets on Fed rises beyond December.

items.headline: Iran's foreign minister says talks with the US are still open and Iran's two-day Hormuz offer still stands
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday, November 21 that Iran is still open to talks with the US and that its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days has not been withdrawn. He set firm conditions, so no deal is close.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28. A framework deal in June broke down over shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane for about a fifth of the world's oil, and the US now blockades Iran's ports. Qatar and Pakistan are carrying messages between the two sides.
beats.happened: Araghchi said Iran's plan still holds: the US lifts its recent sanctions on day one, and Iran reopens the strait and formal talks begin on day two. He said Washington's reply was unfavourable, that Iran wants signs the US is serious first, and that any deal must meet Iran's seven conditions, including keeping its enriched uranium at home. President Donald Trump said on Friday, November 20 that Iran wants a deal, but not one he can accept.
beats.means: Both sides say they want a deal but neither is moving, so the offer gives a path to reopening the strait without making it likely soon.
beats.fx: A small hint of a way out for the oil war premium, outweighed for now by the weekend's attacks.

impact.why: An open offer to reopen Hormuz points to lower oil if accepted, but the US has turned it down so far.
Japan buys most of its oil from the Gulf, so any real progress on Hormuz would ease pressure on the yen.

items.watch: Whether the US answers through Qatar or Pakistan, or lifts any sanctions, which would be the first step in Iran's plan.

items.headline: Gold falls toward $3,500 as the US stock slide drags metals down with it
items.story_title: Gold vs Fed rate rises
items.summary: Gold kept sliding into the close on Friday, November 20, ending near $3,540 an ounce after a brief dip to its lowest since September 2025. Silver fell harder, by almost 4%.

beats.was: Gold set a record in January and held up for months on the war with Iran. Since then, expected Federal Reserve rate rises and a strong dollar have pulled it down, because gold pays no interest.
beats.happened: Gold kept falling into the US close as the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% and slipped more than 10% below its October 6 record. Minutes of the Fed's October meeting showed nearly all officials expect more rate rises, and futures lean to a quarter-point rise at the December 8-9 meeting.
beats.means: Gold did not act as a safe place during the stock slide. Investors sold it alongside shares, likely to raise cash, while rate-rise bets kept the cost of holding it high. A lower 10-year US yield, near 4.94%, gave it no lift.
beats.fx: Pressure on gold. The same Fed rate bets keep the US dollar firm, though falling US yields soften that edge a little.

impact.why: Sold with stocks and held down by expected Fed rate rises, at a 14-month low.
The Fed rate bets that weigh on gold also support the dollar.

items.watch: Whether gold holds near $3,500 when trading reopens on Monday, November 23, and whether central banks step in to buy at these lower prices.

items.headline: Most economists expect a Bank of Japan rate rise to 1.50% in December, with Tokyo prices due Thursday, November 26
items.story_title: Will the Bank of Japan raise rates in December?
items.summary: 61 of 71 economists in a Reuters poll expect the Bank of Japan to raise its rate to 1.50% at its December 17-18 meeting. Tokyo's November consumer prices, due on Thursday, November 26, are the next clue.

beats.was: The yen sits near 159 per dollar because US rates are far higher than Japan's, and Japan's national inflation for October came in below forecasts at 2.2% for the core measure.
beats.happened: A weekly preview from Newsquawk notes the poll result and that Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda has said the bank expects to keep raising rates. Tokyo's November price figures land on Thursday, November 26, and Japan's markets are shut for a holiday on Monday, November 23.
beats.means: A December rise is largely expected, so the yen needs a firm Tokyo figure or a clear signal from the Bank of Japan to gain much from it.
beats.fx: Mild support for the yen if Tokyo prices are firm, while the wide gap with US rates still holds it down.

impact.why: Most economists see a December rate rise, which slowly narrows the gap with US rates.

items.watch: Tokyo's core inflation on Thursday, November 26. A drop below 2% would cast doubt on a December rise.

items.headline: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: US stocks closed sharply lower on Friday, November 20: the S&P 500 fell 3.7% and is now more than 10% below its October high, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 5.3%, wiping out its gain for 2026. Nvidia lost almost 14%.

beats.was: Shares of companies tied to artificial intelligence had carried US stocks to records in early October. Over the past two weeks worries that AI spending has run ahead of profits, plus US midterm election results seen as slowing data-center building, have pulled them down day after day.
beats.happened: The S&P 500 closed at about 6,910, the Dow Jones index fell 1.9% and the Nasdaq composite fell 5.3%, led by a 13.8% drop in chipmaker Nvidia. Anthropic, which only recently listed on the stock market, fell 9% but stayed above its listing price. Buyers moved into US government bonds, pulling the 10-year yield down to about 4.93% from 5.04%.
beats.means: A fall of more than 10% from a peak is a correction, and the Nasdaq's slide is one of its largest single-day drops in years. When stocks fall this hard, money tends to move toward safe places, and lower US bond yields slightly narrow the rate gap that has been lifting the dollar.
beats.fx: Supports the Japanese yen and Swiss franc as safe places to park money, and weighs on the Australian and New Zealand dollars, which tend to fall when investors pull back from risk. The US dollar gets mixed pressure: some safe-haven demand, but lower yields.

impact.why: A deep stock sell-off and falling US yields both favour the yen.
Risk-sensitive currency hit as investors cut exposure to growth.
Moves with global risk appetite, which dropped sharply.
Some demand for the franc as a safe place during the sell-off.
Safe-haven buying offsets lower US bond yields.

items.watch: Whether the selling spreads to Asian and European stocks when markets reopen on Monday, November 23, and whether Federal Reserve officials soften their talk of more rate rises because of it.

items.headline: Itchy trigger fingers sparked Friday gain in oil prices
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Oil recovered from an early drop of almost $5 to close higher on Friday, November 20, with Brent at $92.57 a barrel and US crude at $83.98, as worry about a wider US-Iran fight returned. Both still fell 4-5% over the week.

beats.was: Oil had been sliding for three weeks because Gulf exports are close to pre-war levels again, even as the war between the US and Iran keeps shipping near the Strait of Hormuz risky.
beats.happened: Prices turned up through the afternoon as the US was reported to be sending a third aircraft carrier to the region, Yemen's Houthi group told people near Saudi Red Sea ports to leave, and reports of tankers hitting mines near Hormuz added to the unease. Brent closed up about 0.6% and US crude about 0.9%.
beats.means: The weekly picture still points to plenty of supply, but the late rebound shows how quickly fear of a bigger military clash can put a floor under prices.
beats.fx: A small support for oil-linked currencies such as the Canadian dollar, and a small cost for big oil importers such as Japan.

impact.why: War worries lifted prices off the day's lows, though the week was still down.
A firmer close helps, but oil still fell over the week.

items.watch: Whether the extra US carrier is followed by strikes on Iran or Houthi attacks on Saudi ports, which would lift oil further.

items.headline: Fed Governor Cook says rates must rise further to bring inflation down
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said on Friday, November 20 that US interest rates are not yet high enough to cool inflation and that the Fed cannot afford to wait. She is the latest of several Fed officials to back more rate rises.

beats.was: The Fed raised rates by a quarter point in September, then held at 3.75% to 4% in October, when Cook was one of two officials who voted for another rise. US inflation has been above the Fed's 2% goal for more than five years.
beats.happened: In a speech prepared for a central bank conference in Chile, Cook said the September rise was not enough, that recent price reports show little sign inflation is easing, and that borrowing conditions are still too loose. She described growth as strong and the job market as solid, and warned that falling behind now could force bigger rises later.
beats.means: With Cook, Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, Governor Christopher Waller and several regional Fed heads all leaning the same way, a rise at the December 8-9 meeting looks close to settled, and the debate is about how many more follow early next year.
beats.fx: Supports the US dollar against most currencies by keeping US rates on a rising path, and weighs on gold, which pays no interest.

impact.why: Another Fed board member backs further rate rises, matching what markets already expect.
Higher expected US rates make holding gold less appealing.

items.watch: The Fed's decision on Wednesday, December 9, and whether officials signal a half-point step or more rises in January.

items.headline: Another tanker catches fire in the Strait of Hormuz as a missile hits Iran's Qeshm Island
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: A tanker leaving the Gulf caught fire after being hit near Oman's Musandam coast on Friday, November 20, and Iranian media said a missile struck Iran's Qeshm Island across the strait. No one was reported hurt.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane between Iran and Oman that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been a war zone for months, and several tankers were reported hit by mines or missiles between Wednesday, November 18 and Friday, November 20.
beats.happened: The UK Maritime Trade Operations, a British navy office that tracks shipping risks, said an outbound tanker about 8 nautical miles north of Khasab was struck by an unknown object and caught fire. Iran's Revolutionary Guards blamed a sea mine. Separately, Iranian media reported a missile hit on Qeshm Island, with no word yet on damage or who fired it.
beats.means: Ships are still being hit almost daily, but oil fell through the week to Friday, November 20 because Gulf exports are flowing close to pre-war levels. A strike on Iranian soil adds a new risk that the fighting widens.
beats.fx: Gives oil a small lift against its slide and adds a little demand for safe places such as the Swiss franc.

impact.why: One more tanker hit and a strike on Iranian land add to supply worries, though so far exports keep flowing.
A wider war would add demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Whether anyone claims the Qeshm strike and whether Iran answers it, and any rise in tanker insurance costs through Hormuz.

items.headline: Chip shares keep falling, the fear gauge tops 30 and US 10-year yields slip under 5%
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: US chip shares fell again on Friday, November 20 after a 5% drop in Tokyo stocks, the VIX fear gauge reached its highest since March, and buyers of safe US government bonds pushed the 10-year yield below 5%.

beats.was: Worry that AI spending has run ahead of profits has hit technology shares around the world since Monday, November 16, and the Dow had lost about 6% by Thursday, November 19. Shaky stocks tend to send money toward safe places such as US government bonds, the yen and the Swiss franc.
beats.happened: Early in New York trading Nvidia fell about 3%, and Micron, Broadcom and AMD lost 4-5%. The Nasdaq 100 slipped while the Dow edged up. The Cboe VIX, which measures expected swings in US stocks, hit about 31 before the open. Tokyo's Nikkei fell about 5% and Taiwan and South Korea's main indexes over 5%. The 10-year US Treasury yield fell about 6 basis points to near 4.99%.
beats.means: Fear is spreading from AI shares into wider markets. Lower US bond yields slightly trim the dollar's rate edge, while safe-place demand helps the yen and franc.
beats.fx: Supports the yen and Swiss franc and weighs on growth-linked currencies such as the Australian and New Zealand dollars. For the dollar the pull is two-way: safe demand helps, lower yields hurt.

impact.why: Falling stocks and lower US yields add safe-place demand for the yen.
A global stock slide hurts currencies tied to world growth.
Safe-place demand helps the franc as fear rises.
Safe demand helps, but US yields below 5% trim its rate edge.

items.watch: Whether the stock slide steadies by the close on Friday, November 20, and Fed Governor Lisa Cook's speech in Chile that afternoon.

items.headline: US shoppers' mood improves in November and their inflation fears ease a full point
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The University of Michigan's final November survey, out on Friday, November 20, showed US consumer mood up to 51.5 from 48.0, and households now expect 3.7% inflation over the next year, down from 4.7%.

beats.was: The US Federal Reserve is expected to raise rates at its December 8-9 meeting because inflation has stayed well above its 2% goal. Fed officials watch what households expect prices to do, since those hopes and fears can feed into wages and prices.
beats.happened: The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index rose to 51.5 in its final November reading, in line with forecasts and up from 48.0 in October, still a low level by history. Expected inflation for the next 12 months fell to 3.7% from 4.7%, and the 5-10 year view eased to 3.3% from 3.5%.
beats.means: Households worry a bit less about prices, which takes a little heat out of the Fed's inflation concern. It does not change the expected December rise, but it gives less support to talk of a bigger half-point move.
beats.fx: A mild drag on the case for the dollar, which still has the rate gap on its side. Gold kept falling after the release, near $3,570 an ounce.

impact.why: Better mood but lower inflation expectations soften talk of a larger Fed rise without changing the December call.
Gold stayed down about 1.5% on the day after the release, still pressed by expected Fed rises.

items.watch: US October inflation figures for spending (the PCE price index) and the Fed's December 8-9 decision.

items.headline: Canada's September shop sales rise 0.8%, but an early October estimate shows a 1.5% drop
items.story_title: Will the Bank of Canada raise rates in December?
items.summary: Statistics Canada said on Friday, November 20 that retail sales rose 0.8% in September, a touch above forecasts, but mostly because petrol cost more. Its early estimate for October points to a 1.5% fall.

beats.was: The Canadian dollar sits near its weakest since April 2025 because markets expect the US Federal Reserve to raise rates faster than the Bank of Canada. Markets put about a two-in-three chance on a Bank of Canada rise in December, so signs of spending strength or weakness matter.
beats.happened: Sales reached C$75.3 billion in September, up 0.8% against forecasts near 0.7%, and August was revised up to 1.4%. Petrol station sales jumped 6.9% on higher prices. Without petrol and cars, sales rose only 0.1%, and the amount of goods bought also rose just 0.1%. The agency's first estimate for October is a 1.5% drop.
beats.means: The headline gain mostly reflects prices, not more shopping, and October looks weak. That gives the Bank of Canada a little less reason to raise rates in December.
beats.fx: No lift for the Canadian dollar, which keeps taking its lead from the wider gap with US rates.

impact.why: Spending growth is mostly higher prices and October looks weak, which softens the case for a December rise.

items.watch: Canada's November jobs report and the Bank of Canada's December rate decision.

items.headline: Oil gives back its early gain and slides toward $90 as Gulf exports recover
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Brent crude dropped about 1.8% to near $90.30 a barrel on Friday, November 20, undoing an early rise, and US oil fell about 2% to near $81.60. Both are set for a third weekly fall.

beats.was: The Iran war cut oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year and pushed prices up. In recent weeks Gulf exports have been coming back, and the International Energy Agency expects more oil than buyers need in the last three months of 2026.
beats.happened: After a small rise in the morning on Houthi missile strikes at Riyadh, prices turned lower as traders focused on Middle East exports running close to their pre-war level. US crude stocks also rose by 3.4 million barrels in the week to November 13. Brent is down about 5% since Friday, November 13. Reports of tankers hitting mines near Hormuz did little to stop the slide.
beats.means: The market now weighs plentiful supply more than the risk of new attacks. Cheaper oil lowers income for oil exporters and eases pressure on import bills for countries that buy oil.
beats.fx: Weighs a little on the Canadian dollar and Norway's krone, which earn from oil, and slightly helps big oil buyers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Recovering Gulf exports and higher US stocks outweigh new attacks on ships.
Lower oil prices cut Canada's export income.
Cheaper oil eases Japan's import bill.

items.watch: Whether Brent holds near $90 into the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29, and any further attacks on tankers near Hormuz.

items.headline: Bundesbank's Nagel sees stronger German growth and says the ECB has to act on inflation
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: Joachim Nagel, head of Germany's central bank and a European Central Bank rate-setter, said on Friday, November 20 that German growth looks close to 1.2% this year and that inflation is too high for the ECB to sit still.

beats.was: Euro-area inflation rose to 4.0% in October, twice the ECB's goal, and markets lean strongly toward an ECB rate rise at the December 17 meeting.
beats.happened: Speaking at a banking conference in Frankfurt, Nagel put German growth this year at about 1.2%, well above the Bundesbank's June forecast of 0.5%. He said inflation is too high even though expectations of future inflation stay steady, and that the ECB needs to do something.
beats.means: A leading voice for tighter policy backs a December rise, and stronger German growth removes one reason to wait.
beats.fx: Gives the euro a little support, though the Federal Reserve's faster rate path still weighs on it more.

impact.why: Firm talk from a senior ECB rate-setter backs the December rise markets already expect.

items.watch: Euro-area flash inflation for November and the ECB decision on December 17.

items.headline: Lagarde's Frankfurt speech urges Europe to act before problems become crises
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde used her keynote at the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt on Friday, November 20 to call for faster action on long-run issues such as a single capital market and Europe's reliance on foreign payment technology.

beats.was: Euro-area inflation is 4%, double the ECB's goal, and markets put about a 9 in 10 chance on a rate rise at the ECB's December 17 meeting. Traders hoped the speech would hint at what comes after December.
beats.happened: The published text, titled "Acting in time", focused on structural topics: a digital euro that could first be issued in 2029 if laws pass by year end, a new platform for settling digital assets, and Europe's dependence on foreign card networks. It was her last appearance at this congress as ECB President.
beats.means: The text offers no new clue on interest rates, so expectations for December and 2027 stay where they were.
beats.fx: Little direct effect on the euro, which keeps taking its lead from expected Federal Reserve rate rises.

impact.why: A speech on long-run reforms leaves December rate bets unchanged.

items.watch: Comments from other ECB officials before the December 17 meeting, and euro-area flash inflation for November.

items.headline: EUR/JPY slides as yen strengthens on hawkish BoJ signals
items.story_title: Will the Bank of Japan raise rates in December?
items.summary: The yen gained in European trading on Friday, November 20, with the euro down to about 174.8 yen, as falling stocks, Tokyo's warnings about fast currency moves and bets on a December Bank of Japan rate rise helped it.

beats.was: The dollar came within a few hundredths of 160 yen on Thursday, November 19, a level where Japan has stepped into the market before. Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama has warned against rapid, one-sided currency moves.
beats.happened: On Friday, November 20 the euro fell to about 174.8 yen and the dollar slipped from just under 160 to about 158.7 yen, as Tokyo stocks dropped about 4.5% and US 10-year yields eased toward 4.97%. A Reuters poll found most economists expect the Bank of Japan to raise its rate to 1.5% on December 18, which markets price at about 85%.
beats.means: The yen is getting support from three places at once: demand for safe places as stocks fall, the risk of Japanese buying near 160, and a likely Bank of Japan rise. Japan's October inflation came in below forecast, which keeps a small doubt over December.
beats.fx: A push higher for the yen, mainly against the euro and the dollar, though US rates remain far above Japan's.

impact.why: Safe-place buying, intervention warnings and a likely December Bank of Japan rise lift the yen.
The euro slips against the yen as stocks fall.

items.watch: Bank of Japan meeting on December 18, and whether the dollar returns toward 160 yen.

items.headline: Iran lines up a tanker convoy at Kharg Island to test the US blockade of its oil
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Satellite images and ship-tracking data reported on Friday, November 20 show more than 14 crewed, Iran-flagged tankers waiting at Kharg Island, set to sail toward the Sea of Oman and test the US Navy's blockade of Iranian oil.

beats.was: Kharg Island handles about 85-90% of Iran's crude exports, and loading there stopped once the US Navy began blocking Iranian oil shipments, cutting Iran's main source of income.
beats.happened: Ship trackers say the tankers have crews and Iranian flags and could leave in the coming days, and one ship-to-ship oil transfer near Kharg was seen with its tracking signal off. People close to Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned online that blocking the ships could bring attacks on Gulf oil sites. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said oil flows through Hormuz are rising.
beats.means: If the tankers get through, more Iranian oil reaches a market that already looks well supplied. If the US Navy stops them, it risks a direct clash at sea and fresh threats to Gulf oil sites.
beats.fx: Pulls oil both ways: more supply if the convoy sails freely, a fresh scare if it is blocked. That swing also touches the Canadian dollar, which tracks oil.

impact.why: Could add Iranian supply or spark a clash at sea, depending on how the US Navy responds.
Canada's export income moves with the oil price.

items.watch: Whether the convoy leaves Kharg and how the US Navy responds, and the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 29.

items.headline: Fed Governor Lisa Cook speaks in Chile as she refuses a White House hearing on firing her
items.story_title: The White House push to remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook
items.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook was set to speak at a conference in Chile on the afternoon of Friday, November 20, her first public remarks since her lawyer said she will not take part in a White House hearing on whether President Trump should fire her.

beats.was: President Donald Trump wants to remove Lisa Cook from the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors over claims about her mortgage applications, which she denies. The White House set up a hearing on the case. Markets watch this fight because a president who can fire Fed officials could press the Fed on rates.
beats.happened: Her lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said on Tuesday, November 17 that she has no duty to join a hearing he calls unfair, and that staying away protects the Fed's independence. He also asked to see the White House's evidence first. The White House has not said whether the hearing will go ahead without her. Senator Elizabeth Warren called it a show trial.
beats.means: Nothing has changed for rates yet, and the Fed still looks set to raise them on December 9. But doubt about how free the Fed is from the White House is a slow-burning risk for trust in US policy.
beats.fx: A small, mostly background drag on the dollar if the fight escalates; it matters more if it ever looks likely to change who sets US rates.

impact.why: A fight over firing a Fed governor raises doubts about the Fed's independence.
Worry about Fed independence adds a little demand for gold as a store of value.

items.watch: Whether Cook says anything about rates or the case in Chile on Friday, November 20, and whether the White House holds the hearing without her.

items.headline: Oil edges up after Houthi missiles hit Riyadh, but heads for a third weekly fall
items.story_title: Oil: Gulf attacks vs returning supply
items.summary: Brent crude rose about 0.6% to near $92.60 on the morning of Friday, November 20 after Houthi missile attacks on the Saudi capital, but it is still on course to lose about 3.5% in the week to Friday, November 20.

beats.was: Oil jumped earlier this year when the war with Iran choked tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. This month it has fallen back as Gulf shipments recovered, with crude flows through the strait back near their pre-war level.
beats.happened: Houthi rebels in Yemen fired missiles at Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, which revived worries about Gulf supply. Brent gained 59 cents and US crude about half that, while some analysts said fears about a slowing economy, as AI shares sell off, are holding prices back.
beats.means: Attacks near the oil fields still give prices a lift, but the bigger trend this month is that supply is getting through. The next big event is the OPEC+ producers' meeting on November 29 on output for 2027.
beats.fx: Firmer oil gives a small lift to the Canadian dollar, Canada being a big oil exporter, while a weekly fall keeps that help modest.

impact.why: Gulf attacks add a small risk premium, though the week is still lower.
A daily bounce helps a little, a third weekly drop does not.

items.watch: Whether attacks hit oil facilities or ships rather than cities, and what OPEC+ decides on November 29.

items.headline: UK retail sales rise 0.7% in October, well above forecasts
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: The amount sold in British shops rose 0.7% in October from September, when economists expected no change, a sign households are still spending despite higher fuel bills and borrowing costs.

beats.was: The Bank of England raised rates in November for the first time in three years, and UK inflation reached 3.6% in October. Consumer confidence had dropped sharply that month, so a weak shopping figure was expected.
beats.happened: The Office for National Statistics said on Friday, November 20 that retail sales volumes rose 0.7% in October, against a forecast of 0.0%. Retailers' own updates were mixed, with some chains reporting a better October and others a softer trend.
beats.means: Stronger spending makes it easier for the Bank of England to keep raising rates, since the economy is coping with higher costs. It partly offsets the softer core inflation reading of Wednesday, November 18, which had cut the odds of a December rise.
beats.fx: A push higher for the pound, especially against the euro, because it supports the case for another Bank of England rise in December.

impact.why: A clear beat on shop sales backs another Bank of England rate rise.
The euro loses a little ground against a firmer pound.

items.watch: Bank of England officials' comments on December, and the UK government budget plans for energy bills.

items.headline: Australia's October inflation figure on Wednesday, November 25 is the last before the RBA's December 8 decision
items.story_title: Will the RBA raise rates again in December?
items.summary: Australia reports October consumer prices on Wednesday, November 25, the last inflation reading before the Reserve Bank of Australia meets on December 8. Prices rose 4.3% over the year to September.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate to 4.85% on November 3 in a 6-3 vote, but Australia then lost jobs for a second month and unemployment rose to 4.9% in October.
beats.happened: The October monthly price report comes out on the morning of Wednesday, November 25 in Sydney, which is the evening of Tuesday, November 24 in the US. September's yearly rate was 4.3%. Forecasts are unclear, with one calendar showing 4.2%.
beats.means: Inflation that stays above 4% would keep another rate rise alive despite the weak jobs data. A clear drop would make a pause on December 8 much more likely.
beats.fx: A preview only. The figure can move the Australian dollar either way.

impact.why: High inflation would revive talk of a December rise, a soft figure would back a pause.
The New Zealand dollar often moves with the Australian dollar on big Australian data.

items.watch: Whether yearly inflation stays above 4%, which keeps a December rise possible, or falls clearly below it.

items.headline: Gold drops to about $3,550 and heads for its worst week since March
items.story_title: Gold vs Fed rate rises
items.summary: Gold fell almost 2% early on Friday, November 20 to about $3,550 an ounce, its lowest since September 2025, and is on course for a fall of close to 9% in the week to Friday, November 20.

beats.was: Gold set a record in January and held up for months on the war with Iran. Since then, expected Federal Reserve rate rises and a strong dollar have pulled it down, since gold pays no interest.
beats.happened: Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said more rate rises are needed because inflation is too high, and futures put the chance of a December rise near certain. Silver, platinum and palladium also fell about 2%.
beats.means: Rising US interest rates make holding gold more costly, and that is outweighing the war as a reason to buy it. The fall picked up speed in the week of November 16.
beats.fx: Pressure on gold, and a mirror of the dollar's strength: the dollar sits near its highest in 19 months.

impact.why: Near-certain Fed rate rises push gold to a 14-month low.
The same rate bets that sink gold keep the dollar near a 19-month high.

items.watch: Whether central banks keep buying on the dip, and US inflation data ahead of the Fed's December 8-9 meeting.

items.headline: Tokyo and Seoul stocks fall about 4.5% as AI worries spread to Asia
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: Japan's Nikkei 225 and South Korea's Kospi each fell about 4.5% on the morning of Friday, November 20, following a 2% drop in US stocks and the sudden resignation of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.

beats.was: US stocks had fallen for five sessions in a row on worries about Federal Reserve rate rises and high prices for AI shares. AI company Anthropic's market debut on Thursday, November 19 went well but did not lift the wider market.
beats.happened: Nvidia, the biggest maker of AI chips, swung from a 4.7% gain to a 3.3% loss on Thursday, November 19 after Huang, its co-founder and chief executive, stepped down without warning. The Dow fell about 1,100 points, and in Asia on Friday, November 20 the Nikkei dropped to about 56,775 and the Kospi to about 4,905, both heavy in chip makers.
beats.means: The pullback from AI shares has become a global selloff, which leaves investors more wary of risk going into the weekend.
beats.fx: A deeper slide in stocks tends to lift the yen and the US dollar as safe places and weigh on the Australian and New Zealand dollars. The dollar still held near 159 yen, so the yen's gain so far is small.

impact.why: A sharp fall in Tokyo stocks adds safe-place demand for the yen.
A global stock selloff hurts a currency tied to world growth.
Risk-shy markets weigh on another growth-linked currency.
Investors seeking safety add some demand for the dollar.

items.watch: Whether European and US stocks keep falling on Friday, November 20, and who Nvidia names to replace Huang.

items.headline: Asian shares head for their worst week since March 2020
items.story_title: AI stocks and the mood in markets
items.summary: MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares fell 2.5% on Friday, November 20, its sixth daily drop, leaving it about 7% down for the week, the worst since the start of the pandemic.

beats.was: Worries that AI shares had risen too far, together with expected Federal Reserve rate rises, have pushed stocks lower all week. AI company Anthropic's market debut on Thursday, November 19 did not change the mood.
beats.happened: Japan's Nikkei 225 lost about 4% and South Korea's Kospi nearly 5% on Friday, November 20. The US dollar index held near 104, close to its highest since April 2025, and the 10-year US Treasury yield stayed just above 5%.
beats.means: The selloff in AI shares has turned into a broad retreat from risk across Asia, with higher US rates making investors less willing to buy the dip.
beats.fx: Weighs on currencies tied to world growth like the Australian dollar, and gives some support to the yen and the US dollar as safe places.

impact.why: A broad Asian stock slide hurts a growth-linked currency.
Risk-shy markets add some safe-place demand for the yen.
The dollar holds near a 19-month high as investors seek safety.

items.watch: Whether European and US stocks stabilise on Friday, November 20 or extend the slide into next week.
